name: Question 14
problem:
The function $g(x)$ is continuous over $x\in [2,7].$ Some values of $g(x)$ are given in the table below. 

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g(x)$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $-3$ | $1$ | $0$ | $2$ |

What is the smallest possible number of solutions to the equation $g(x)=-1?$
worked_solution:
Since $g$ is a continuous function on $[2,7]$, we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of $[2,7].$

So, we will go through each subinterval of $[2,7]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1.$

- On the subinterval $[2,3],$ we have $g(2)=-2$ and $g(3)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-2,1],$  the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[3,4],$ we have $g(3)=1$ and $g(4)=-3.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[4,5],$ we have $g(4)=-3$ and $g(5)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[5,6],$ we have $g(5)=1$ and $g(6)=0.$ Since $-1\notin [0,1],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[6,7],$ we have $g(6)=0$ and $g(7)=2.$ Since $-1\notin [0,2],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $g(x)=-1$ on the subintervals $[2,3],$ $[3,4]$  and $[4,5].$ Therefore, $g(x)=-1$ has at least three solutions on $[2,7].$

Question 14
?

The function g(x) is continuous over x∈[2,7]. Some values of g(x) are given in the table below.

x 2 3 4 5 6 7
g(x) −2 1 −3 1 0 2

What is the smallest possible number of solutions to the equation g(x)=−1?

a
0
b
4
c
3
d
2
e
1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since g is a continuous function on [2,7], we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of [2,7].

So, we will go through each subinterval of [2,7] and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation g(x)=−1.

  • On the subinterval [2,3], we have g(2)=−2 and g(3)=1. Since −1∈[−2,1], the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation g(x)=−1 on this subinterval.

  • On the subinterval [3,4], we have g(3)=1 and g(4)=−3. Since −1∈[−3,1], the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation g(x)=−1 on this subinterval.

  • On the subinterval [4,5], we have g(4)=−3 and g(5)=1. Since −1∈[−3,1], the IVT does guarantee a solution to the equation g(x)=−1 on this subinterval.

  • On the subinterval [5,6], we have g(5)=1 and g(6)=0. Since −1∉[0,1], the IVT does not guarantee a solution to the equation g(x)=−1 on this subinterval.

  • On the subinterval [6,7], we have g(6)=0 and g(7)=2. Since −1∉[0,2], the IVT does not guarantee a solution to the equation g(x)=−1 on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to g(x)=−1 on the subintervals [2,3], [3,4] and [4,5]. Therefore, g(x)=−1 has at least three solutions on [2,7].
